blocks.text: Nobody has ever seen a cat fall from a Nigerian sky, yet "it is raining cats and dogs" is perfectly clear to every English speaker. Idioms mean something other than what their words say — and they are frozen. Change one word and the expression breaks.

blocks.title: Idiom
blocks.text: A fixed group of words whose meaning cannot be worked out from the individual words. *Beat about the bush* has nothing to do with bushes; it means to avoid the main point. Because the expression is fixed, its wording cannot be altered.

blocks.title: Collocation
blocks.text: A pair or group of words that habitually go together: *heavy rain*, *strong wind*, *thick fog*, *make a decision*, *do homework*. The combination is not logical but conventional — English speakers simply say it that way.

let the cat out of the bag

a great fuss over something trivial

blocks.markdown:
### Collocations you are expected to know

**make** a decision, an effort, a mistake, progress, an appointment, a promise
**do** homework, business, one's best, a favour, harm, research
**take** a photograph, a risk, an examination, medicine, notes
**pay** attention, a visit, a compliment, respect
**heavy** rain, traffic, smoker, meal — but **strong** wind, tea, coffee, argument

The verb *make* and the verb *do* cause more errors than any other pair. "Do a decision" and "make my homework" are both wrong, and no amount of reasoning will produce the right partner — only exposure will.

blocks.title: Working out an unfamiliar idiom from its context
blocks.prompt: What does the idiom mean here? "After two failed appeals, the lawyer finally threw in the towel."

steps.text: Refuse the literal reading first. No towel is involved in an appeal court, so the expression must be figurative.
Look for the situation the sentence describes. Two appeals have already failed, so the lawyer has run out of options.
Note the signal word *finally*, which tells you this is the last step in a sequence of attempts.
Ask what a person does when every attempt has failed. The natural answer is that the person stops trying.
Check the origin if you know it. The image comes from boxing, where a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop the fight — an admission of defeat.
State the meaning in your own words: he gave up the struggle and accepted defeat.

blocks.answer: He gave up the struggle — the sequence of failed appeals plus *finally* points to surrender rather than a change of tactics

blocks.title: Never half-remember an idiom
blocks.text: *Raining cat and dog*, *a storm in the teacup*, *at my wit end* — each of these is a broken idiom, and a broken idiom is worse in an essay than plain language. If you are not certain of the exact wording, write the plain meaning instead: "it was raining very heavily".

items: Phrasal verbs behave like idioms: the particle carries the meaning. *Take after* means resemble; *take up* means begin; *take on* means accept; *take over* means assume control.
Some collocations fix the preposition too: *at short notice*, *on purpose*, *in a hurry*, *by mistake*.
Idioms are informal in tone, so use them sparingly in a formal letter and freely in a narrative essay.
Nigerian English has idioms of its own, such as *put to bed* for giving birth, but examinations require the Standard English forms.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: When an idiom is unfamiliar, do not guess from one word inside it. Read the whole sentence and ask what situation is being described; then choose the option that fits the situation. The literal reading of the image is nearly always one of the distractors.

points: An idiom's meaning cannot be deduced from its individual words.
Idioms are fixed, so changing even one word breaks the expression.
Collocations are conventional partnerships such as *heavy rain* and *make a decision*.
The verbs *make* and *do* have separate fixed partners that must be memorised.
In phrasal verbs the particle changes the meaning completely.
If unsure of an idiom's exact wording, write the plain meaning instead.
Use the situation described in the sentence to work out an unfamiliar idiom.
